rationale:
Cal.com's v2 API and hosted MCP server together document the full agent workflow: querying available slots (docs-2/23/38), creating bookings (docs-1/37), rescheduling (docs-3/24/39), and webhook triggers show BOOKING_CANCELLED events (docs-5/26/42) alongside an explicit agents.md guide (docs-12/17/31/45/46) and a live, runtime-verified MCP server (cal-com-probe-rt-1) enabling natural-language booking management without a dashboard (docs-30). The public booking endpoint requiring no auth further supports autonomous agent booking (docs-46).
missing for 10: an explicit first-party 'cancel a booking' endpoint doc (only inferred via webhook triggers) and independent/hands-on confirmation that an agent can complete the full cycle end-to-end via MCP.

Cal.com publishes an official hosted MCP server (mcp.cal.com) explicitly for connecting AI clients to scheduling via MCP, confirmed live via runtime probe with proper OAuth handshake, plus a dedicated agents.md doc detailing how AI agents can check availability, create bookings, manage event types, and query slots via the API/CLI as an alternative tool-calling surface. Missing for 10: independent third-party (non-vendor) hands-on report of using the MCP server successfully in a real agent workflow.

Cal.com publishes a live llms.txt (confirmed via HTTP 200 probe) plus a dedicated agent-oriented docs page (cal.com/docs/agents.md) with explicit guidance for AI agents (availability checks, booking creation, CLI recommendation for command-executing agents), and a documentation index at /docs/llms.txt for deeper crawling. Missing for 10: no independent third-party report of an agent actually consuming llms.txt end-to-end to complete a task.

The evidence pack documents Cal.com's API/MCP server enabling AI agents to check availability, create bookings, and manage event types — but this is about external agents *acting on* Cal.com data, not the product itself surfacing AI-generated insights or suggestions from a user's scheduling data (e.g., analytics, pattern detection, smart recommendations) within its own UI. No such in-product AI insights feature is mentioned anywhere in the pack.

Cal.com provides webhooks (event-triggered automations like BOOKING_CREATED, RESCHEDULED, CANCELLED), a full API/MCP server for AI agents to check availability and create bookings, and workflows are mentioned in docs — enabling background automation without human intervention. However, evidence centers on event-driven/reactive triggers (webhooks fire on booking events) and agent-invoked actions rather than a native scheduled/cron-style 'run autonomously on a timer' automation builder, and there's no hands-on confirmation of long-running unattended agent workflows in production. missing for 10: evidence of a dedicated scheduled/cron automation engine (vs event-triggered webhooks only), independent/hands-on proof of autonomous background execution over time, and detail on the 'workflows' feature's automation depth.

The evidence describes Cal.com's API and MCP server that let *external* AI agents/clients control Cal.com (bookings, availability, event types), but there is no evidence of a built-in AI assistant feature inside the Cal.com product UI itself that a user can delegate tasks to. This is an agent-enablement/API story, not a native in-product assistant.

Cal.com ships a full REST API v2 with auth via API key/OAuth, CLI recommendation for headless agents, a public booking endpoint requiring no auth for agent use, and explicit docs (cal.com/docs/agents.md) describing headless automation patterns for AI agents/CI; self-hosting is also confirmed to work via probe evidence. missing for 10: independent third-party CI pipeline case study, and community friction around self-hosted API/docker reliability (comm-3, comm-4, comm-11) tempers confidence slightly.

Cal.com's AI-native story is that it exposes its own scheduling tools TO AI agents (via API v2 and the hosted MCP server at mcp.cal.com), not that Cal.com itself acts as an MCP client host that plugs in external MCP servers to use their tools. All evidence describes Cal.com as the MCP server/tool provider, none shows it consuming other MCP servers, so this client-side axis is a category mismatch for a scheduling SaaS product.

Cal.com documents an official hosted MCP server (mcp.cal.com) and local instance option, explicitly for connecting AI clients via natural language to manage bookings/event types/schedules, and a runtime probe confirms the hosted server is live and speaks MCP OAuth. Missing for 10: independent third-party hands-on report of a full agent session using the MCP server beyond vendor docs and a single runtime probe.

Cal.com ships an official hosted MCP server (mcp.cal.com) explicitly documented to let users 'manage bookings, event types, schedules, and more through natural language in any MCP-compatible client,' plus a dedicated agents.md guide enabling AI agents to check availability, create bookings, and manage event types via the API. A runtime probe confirms the hosted MCP endpoint is live and speaking the MCP OAuth flow, corroborating the docs. Missing for 10: independent/community hands-on validation that natural-language commands work end-to-end in a real MCP client (only vendor docs and a protocol-level probe are available).

Missing for 10: CLI documentation/README, install instructions, command reference, and any hands-on or community confirmation of the CLI in use.

Cal.com publishes an extensive, well-documented public REST API v2 (bookings, event types, slots, schedules, webhooks, conferencing apps, routing traces) with multiple auth methods (OAuth, API key), plus a dedicated agents.md guide explicitly targeting AI-driven usage and a hosted MCP server for natural-language control. Missing for 10: explicit AI-agent-facing documentation/example of creating or managing recurring bookings via MCP or agents.md, and independent/hands-on confirmation that recurring booking creation works reliably through the AI-agent flow.

The evidence pack covers bookings, event types, scheduling, webhooks, and MCP/agent integration, but nothing describes version history, review workflows, or rollback capabilities for Cal.com's automations (workflows/webhooks). Community reviews confirm real-world usage as a Calendly alternative for exactly this workflow. Missing for 10: independent hands-on verification of the actual booking-link UX/flow (evidence is docs-heavy) and no direct end-user review specifically praising the no-back-and-forth booking experience itself.

Missing for 10: independent hands-on confirmation of webhook delivery reliability/latency from a third party.

Closest items (cal-com-docs-6/27 on schedules, cal-com-docs-4 on event duration) do not address these limit features.

Missing for 10: dedicated collective-event-type configuration docs analogous to the round-robin config docs, and independent/hands-on confirmation that collective slot-blocking works as described.

Cal.com exposes webhooks (BOOKING_CREATED, BOOKING_PAID, BOOKING_RESCHEDULED, etc.) and a general-purpose API/OAuth layer that could feed a CRM or Zapier via automation, and routing-form docs reference 'CRM lookups' and 'CRM fallback' in host-selection logic, plus an 'app store of integrations' is claimed. However, there is no direct evidence of a native Salesforce, HubSpot, or Zapier app/connector, nor of an out-of-the-box no-code integration flow — only the building blocks (webhooks + API) that a sales lead would need someone to wire up. Missing for 10: explicit documentation or listing of a Salesforce/HubSpot/Zapier native app, an official Zapier integration page, and any hands-on/independent confirmation that bookings actually sync into these CRMs.

A Cal.com cofounder explicitly states in community discussion that everything that is Calendly's paid 'Pro' tier is free on Cal.com, and general docs describe core one-on-one scheduling/booking-link functionality that would presumably be available without payment; however, other community comments note certain paid add-ons (e.g., $29/mo premium usernames) exist, and there is no first-party pricing-page or plan-limits documentation in the pack confirming exactly what's free. Missing for 10: explicit documentation of Google/Outlook/Apple calendar integrations, description of two-way sync/conflict-avoidance mechanics, and independent corroboration that double-booking is prevented across multiple connected calendars.

However, there is no evidence of complete parity: documentation doesn't explicitly confirm API coverage for workflows, payments configuration, or app-store integration management that exist in the UI, and community reports flag friction around self-hosting the API itself (comm-3), suggesting some UI capabilities may not be fully API-exposed or freely accessible. missing for 10: explicit confirmation that workflows/payments/app-store UI features are API-manipulable, and independent verification of full API-UI feature parity beyond scheduling core.

Cal.com's API (v2) exposes bookings, event types, schedules, and webhooks, and the MIT-licensed Cal.diy fork plus self-hosting option (with own DB per cal-com-comm-12) give a path to full data ownership rather than lock-in — supporting an 'export and leave' capability indirectly. However, there is no documented dedicated data-export feature (e.g., bulk export to CSV/JSON) and community reports dispute how independent self-hosting really is, with claims you 'can't self-host the API' and must pay to use it (cal-com-comm-3), and Docker images being restricted/removed for the OSS edition (cal-com-comm-14, cal-com-comm-19). Missing for 10: an explicit bulk data-export tool/format, clear confirmation that self-hosted instances are fully independent of hosted API, and resolution of the docker-image/self-host restriction disputes.

However, evidence also shows cal.diy explicitly strips 'enterprise/commercial code' from the main Cal.com repo (implying some features are closed-source) and community reports describe the AGPL as 'restrictive' and cite a 'bait-and-switch' reducing self-host support, which tempers but does not negate the underlying open-source readability of the codebase. Missing for 10: confirmation the entire feature set (including enterprise pieces) is open rather than split, and resolution of community concerns about license restrictiveness/trust.

However, concrete hands-on community evidence directly contradicts current self-hosting viability: Cal.com stopped publishing public Docker images and told users to build the image themselves (cal-com-comm-4, cal-com-comm-14, cal-com-comm-19), the docs now say self-hosting is 'strictly recommended for personal, non-production use' (cal-com-comm-15), the API itself cannot be self-hosted without paying (cal-com-comm-3), the docker-compose setup is broken/messy (cal-com-comm-11), and the Cal.diy fork had no published Docker tags at time of the runtime probe (cal-com-probe-rt-2) — with users describing this as a 'bait and switch' (cal-com-comm-15, cal-com-comm-16, cal-com-comm-18). Missing for 10: a working, currently-published self-host Docker image/instructions for Cal.diy, first-party confirmation that self-hosting is production-supported, and resolution of the API self-hosting restriction.

Missing for 10: dedicated Stripe/payment-app integration docs, API examples showing price/currency fields on event-type creation, and independent/hands-on verification of a successful paid booking flow.
